reference.source: American Academy of Sleep Medicine ICSD-3
clinicalPearls: Defined by chronic excessive daytime sleepiness with cataplexy and/or a low cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin (orexin) level
Cataplexy is a sudden transient loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, classically laughter, with preserved consciousness
Other features include sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations and disrupted nocturnal sleep
It is strongly associated with the HLA-DQB1*06:02 allele, supporting an autoimmune basis for hypocretin-neuron loss
The multiple sleep latency test typically shows a short sleep latency and two or more sleep-onset REM periods
Management combines scheduled naps and sleep hygiene with wake-promoting agents and specific anticataplectic treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Narcolepsy type 1 is caused by selective loss of the hypocretin (orexin)-producing neurons of the lateral hypothalamus, which normally stabilise wakefulness and suppress inappropriate REM sleep. The deficiency is believed to be autoimmune, occurring in genetically susceptible individuals carrying HLA-DQB1*06:02, sometimes after immune triggers. Loss of hypocretin signalling destabilises the boundaries between wake and REM sleep, producing sleepiness and intrusion of REM phenomena such as cataplexy, sleep paralysis and dream-like hallucinations into wakefulness.
additionalInvestigations: Overnight polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test
Cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin measurement where available
HLA typing as a supportive test
Assessment to exclude other causes of hypersomnolence
Sleep diary and actigraphy to confirm adequate prior sleep
redFlags: Sleepiness severe enough to impair driving or safety-critical tasks
Rapid weight gain or precocious features in children
Atypical features suggesting a secondary hypothalamic lesion
reference.prognosis: Narcolepsy type 1 is a lifelong condition, but most patients achieve meaningful control of sleepiness and cataplexy with combined behavioural and pharmacological treatment.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis by not recognising emotionally triggered cataplexy
Performing the multiple sleep latency test without ensuring adequate prior sleep
Attributing cataplexy to syncope or seizures
references: American Academy of Sleep Medicine ICSD-3
Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine
management: Establish behavioural foundations with scheduled naps, consistent sleep-wake timing and good sleep hygiene
Treat excessive daytime sleepiness with wake-promoting agents such as modafinil, armodafinil, pitolisant or solriamfetol, or with stimulants such as methylphenidate or amfetamines
Treat cataplexy specifically with sodium oxybate, pitolisant or anticataplectic antidepressants such as SNRIs, SSRIs or tricyclics, with sodium oxybate also improving disrupted nocturnal sleep
Counsel on driving safety and the occupational implications of sleep attacks and cataplexy
Screen for and manage comorbid depression, obesity and disturbed nocturnal sleep
Confirm the diagnosis with polysomnography, multiple sleep latency testing and, where needed, cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin measurement, under sleep-medicine specialist care
Provide lifelong follow-up with pharmacological titration and support
